title: Infra GPU capacity, cloud accounts & networking, IaC modules, and CI/CD ops guide
author: Ravi Shah
body:
Summary

This document consolidates operational guidance for the infra engineering team on (1) GPU fleet and capacity planning, (2) cloud accounts and networking patterns for inference workloads, (3) Terraform / IaC module best practices and examples, (4) CI/CD build pipelines for infra artifacts, and (5) runbook steps for common capacity and networking incidents. The goal is to provide a single on-call and onboarding reference so engineers can reliably manage Redwood's inference fleet and provisioning pipelines.

Intended audience
- Infra engineers and on-call SREs
- Platform and serving runtime owners
- Security/networking engineers helping private deployments

High-level goals
- Maintain GPU utilization in target range while meeting latency SLOs
- Keep provisioning lead time < 6 hours for predictable growth and < 2 hours for critical bursts
- Ensure reproducible, auditable IaC and CI/CD processes for cloud accounts and VPC networking
- Provide clear runbooks for capacity incidents, account onboarding, and rollback procedures

Ownership and contact points
- GPU fleet capacity (owner): Lucas Rivera (eng-infra-gpu)
- Cloud accounts & networking (owner): Maya Li (eng-infra-networking)
- IaC / Terraform modules (owner): Ravi Shah (infra-iac)
- CI/CD pipelines & builds (owner): Evan Thompson (infra-ci)
- On-call rotation: infra-sre on-call rota (see /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets)

1) GPU fleet and capacity planning

Overview
We operate a multi-region GPU fleet split by service tier (hosted, dedicated, private). Capacity planning must balance utilization, burstability, and headroom for canaries/rollouts. The infra team maintains autoscaling policies and reserved pools per customer tier.

Key metrics and SLOs
- Target average GPU utilization (p95 across fleet): 60-75%
- Queue time SLO: p95 request queue time < 100 ms for hosted-high tier
- Scale-up latency: median time to add a GPU instance to pool < 5 minutes (target)
- Scale-down delay: 10 minutes cooldown to avoid thrash
- Cost target: cost-per-token improvement targets are tracked monthly in the Optimize dashboard

Capacity thresholds and alerts
- Alert: Cluster free capacity < 15% for > 10m - paging to infra-sre primary
- Alert: Queue time p95 > 200 ms for 5m - page infra-sre and serving-runtime owner
- Alert: GPU OOM rate > 0.5% of requests in 10m - page serving-runtime and infra-gpu owners

Scaling policy examples
- Predictable batch: scheduled scale based on historical daily patterns (Terraform-managed schedule)
- Reactive: autoscaler based on queue latency + pod pending time (Kubernetes/Taints + custom controller)
- Burst pool: small burstable on-demand pool (region-specific) with automated fallback routing to cheaper model variant when burst capacity exhausted

Capacity runbook: high queue time (p95 > 200ms)
1. Acknowledge the alert and post to #infra-ops with the alert link and recent graph links (Grafana).
2. Check region and service tags: which pool (hosted/dedicated/private).
3. Verify autoscaler activity: kubectl get hpa / custom-autoscaler status; check controller logs.
4. If autoscaler failed to scale: check quota (cloud account) and instance availability.
   - Run: gcloud compute reservations list --filter=region=... (or AWS equivalent)
5. If instance shortages or quota: open cloud quota request or initiate standby allocation from burst pool.
6. If scaling is occurring but queue persists: inspect model latency regressions (serving-runtime dashboards) and consider temporary routing to a compatible model variant.
7. Communicate: update incident channel with ETA and mitigation steps.
8. Post-incident: create postmortem if SLO breached; include timeline and capacity changes.

2) Cloud accounts & networking patterns

Account structure and governance
- We use a two-tier account model per cloud provider: central management account (billing + IAM) and environment accounts (prod, staging, dev).
- Each customer private deployment maps to a dedicated account or VPC as required by contract.
- All account creation requests use the account provisioning pipeline (see CI/CD section) and require owner approval.

Networking patterns
- VPC design: regional VPCs with isolated subnets per service tier. Public-facing gateways are limited to ingress controllers; inference compute sits in private subnets with NAT egress rules restricted to approved endpoints.
- Transit: we use transit gateway / VPC peering for cross-account access and control plane connectivity with strict routing tables and security groups.
- Private deployments: leverage Transit + Customer VPN or Direct Connect for low-latency on-prem access.

Security controls
- Egress allowlist for model artifact downloads and container registries.
- KMS-backed key policies for secrets and disk encryption.
- Flow logs enabled on all inference subnets with 30-day retention; critical flows ship to long-term archive.

Account onboarding runbook
1. Request: Open an account request ticket in the infra account provisioning queue with business justification and required quotas.
2. Approvals: infra-networking and security must sign off.
3. Provisioning: CI/CD pipeline creates account, sets baseline IAM roles and SCPs (for AWS), and deploys baseline network Terraform modules.
4. Validation: run automated tests (VPC reachability, NAT, NACLs, KMS access).
5. Handover: add account to billing dashboards, create runbooks for customer-specific networking (if private deployment).

3) Terraform / IaC module practices

Standards
- All modules live in the infra-iac monorepo and follow semantic versioning.
- Modules must be small, composable, and documented. Each module requires a README with inputs, outputs, example usage, and owners.
- Changes to public modules must go through a design review (ADR) if they are >patch.

Module testing
- Unit: terratest / kitchen-terraform tests run in CI for each module change.
- Integration: smoke apply in ephemeral sandbox account created per PR.
- Linting: terraform fmt + tflint + checkov in CI.

Example: GPU node pool module (excerpt)
```hcl
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/infra-iac/modules/gpu-node-pool.git?ref=v1.4.0"
  name   = "gpu-pool-${var.region}"
  region = var.region
  gpu_type = "nvidia-a100"
  min_size = 2
  max_size = 200
  taints = [{ key = "dedicated", value = "gpu", effect = "NO_SCHEDULE" }]
}
```

Change control
- Non-breaking changes: PR + CI + maintainer merge.
- Breaking changes (removing inputs/outputs or altering semantics): open ADR, communicate to owners, and coordinate a major version bump with migration guide.

4) CI/CD & build pipelines for infra artifacts

Pipeline templates
- Module PR pipeline: terraform fmt -> tflint -> unit tests (terratest) -> plan in ephemeral account -> approval gate -> apply to shared staging.
- Account provisioning pipeline: triggers when a new account ticket is approved; creates account resources, baseline IAM, VPC, and required quotas.
- AMI/container build pipeline: Packer build (AMI) / Docker build -> vulnerability scan -> push to registry -> sign artifact -> trigger deployment pipeline.

Example CI commands (GitHub Actions snippet)
```yaml
- name: TF fmt
  run: terraform fmt -check
- name: Lint
  run: tflint --module
- name: Unit tests
  run: go test ./test -v
- name: Plan
  run: terraform plan -out=tfplan
```

Secrets and approvals
- All pipeline secrets stored in the central secrets manager (KMS-backed). Approvals for production applies require two approvers from the infra team.

Release cadence
- Module patches: continuous
- Module minor/major: quarterly planning with a changelog and migration notes

5) Operational runbooks (common incidents)

Incident: GPU instance preemption on cloud provider
1. Pager triggers for increased queue and node termination events.
2. Check cloud provider event stream (gcloud / aws health) for preemption notices.
3. Evacuate running pods with graceful termination and requeue requests where possible.
4. If % of preempted nodes > 10% of pool: scale up replacement nodes using reserved capacity or trigger burst pool.
5. For repeated preemptions: add preemption-aware annotations to workloads and prefer reserved/bare-metal instances for critical pools.

Incident: VPC route leak / misconfigured route table
1. Post to #infra-ops and isolate the affected VPC (remove peering / detach problematic route).
2. Run validation: ip route table check and flow logs to identify leak sources.
3. Rollback last network change (CI/CD) and redeploy correct Terraform state.
4. Verify connectivity for control plane and data plane; notify impacted customers.

Post-incident and follow-up
- Every incident that triggers an SLO breach must have a postmortem within 72 hours with timeline, root cause, and action items.
- Track corrective actions in the infra backlog and assign owners + ETA.

Appendices
A. Useful CLI commands
- Check node autoscaler: kubectl get hpa -n infra || kubectl get deployment -n infra
- Inspect pending pods: kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o wide
- Check cloud quotas: gcloud compute regions describe REGION --format=json or aws service-quotas get-service-quota

B. Useful links
- Module repo: git@repo/infra-iac/modules
- Grafana dashboards: https://grafana.internal/redwood/infra-gpu
- CI pipelines: https://ci.internal.redwood/workflows/infra

C. Revision history
- 2025-11-15: Created (Ravi Shah)
- 2026-01-20: Added runbook steps for preemption; updated autoscaler thresholds (Maya Li)
- 2026-03-01: Clarified account onboarding pipeline and reviewers list (Evan Thompson)

Please use this page as the canonical infra ops guide for GPU fleet and related provisioning workflows. Link any playbook updates back to the appropriate module READMEs and notify reviewers for major changes.
